articles.title: Why Jamaica is seeking $10bn in reparations from the UK
articles.summary: Hundreds of thousands of enslaved Africans toiled in Jamaica under more than 300 years of British rule.
articles.body:
A Jamaican delegation to the United Kingdom has said it will file a petition addressed to King Charles III to seek legal guidance on the question of slavery reparations.

This is the first time a British Commonwealth state will use this legal route “for the cause of reparatory justice”, the Jamaican delegation said, as the visit to London kicks off on Monday. King Charles is Jamaica’s head of state, as the country is yet to transition from a constitutional monarchy to a republic.

The Jamaican government estimates that the country is owed about $10bn, but the UK has repeatedly refused to pay for historical slavery.

What is the latest petition all about, and how will the UK respond?

What are Jamaica and the UK’s relations like?

Jamaica’s relations with the UK stem back to 1655 when it became an English colony. Hundreds of thousands of enslaved African people toiled in Jamaica under more than 300 years of British rule and faced brutal conditions.

In August 1962, after Jamaica became independent, it established diplomatic ties with the UK and also became a member of the Commonwealth of Nations, an international political association of 56 member countries made up of former British colonies.

The UK and Jamaica are also major trade partners, with UK exports to Jamaica reaching about $222m in 2025 and UK imports from Jamaica reaching about $76m.

While Jamaica has been independent since 1962, it has continued to recognise the British monarch as its head of state. But in recent years, calls to ditch the British king as Jamaica’s head of state have grown.

In March 2022, Jamaican activists, as well as prominent professors, politicians and other leaders, rejected a visit by the duke and duchess of Cambridge, calling on the United Kingdom to apologise and pay reparations for hundreds of years of slavery.

In an open letter published before the British royal couple’s arrival, 100 Jamaican leaders had said they saw “no reason to celebrate” the Queen’s coronation “because her leadership, and that of her predecessors, have perpetuated the greatest human rights tragedy in the history of humankind”.

“During her 70 years on the throne, your grandmother has done nothing to redress and atone for the suffering of our ancestors that took place during her reign and/or during the entire period of British trafficking of Africans, enslavement, indentureship and colonialization,” the letter read.

In December 2024, the Jamaican government also tabled a constitutional amendment bill in parliament to replace the British king as the head of state.

What is Jamaica’s latest petition about?

In June last year, Jamaica formally raised a petition addressed to the British monarch seeking slavery reparations.

On Monday, Jamaica’s Ministry of Culture, Gender, Entertainment and Sport said its minister, Olivia Grange, is expected to lead the country’s delegation “to advance Jamaica’s push for reparations for the African ancestors who suffered under hundreds of years of enslavement” in London.

The ministry added that it would meet with the British Museum to discuss “the repatriation of cultural artefacts taken from Jamaica”.

The petition will ask the king, Jamaica’s head of state, to answer three questions on the transatlantic slave trade to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, the Caribbean island’s highest court of appeal based in London.

Under the Judicial Committee Act of 1833, the UK monarch has the authority to refer legal matters to the court for an advisory opinion.

The questions include: whether the enslavement of Africans in Jamaica was legal under English common law, whether it violated international law, and whether the UK has a legal obligation to provide a remedy for the harm caused by slavery.

“We want the answers. Once we get the answers, or once we get a response to those questions, then the next steps will be determined,” Grange said.

Olivette Otele, a historian and distinguished research professor of the Legacies and Memory of Slavery at SOAS University of London, told Al Jazeera that the king’s role in the process was symbolic.

“He doesn’t make any decisions. So it’s really up to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council and also the British government to respond to this petition. My sense is that they’re going to say that enslavement was not legal under English law,” she said.

Have other countries also sought reparations from the UK?

In recent years, several Commonwealth nations have been demanding that the UK pay reparations for its role in the transatlantic slave trade.

At a meeting in Samoa in October 2024 for the biennial Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM), Commonwealth leaders said they would proceed with “plans to examine reparatory justice” for the slave trade.

At the summit, Bahamian Prime Minister Philip Davis had said it was time for the Commonwealth to seek “justice” for the brutal history of slavery.

“Let’s have a conversation about this … We all appreciate this, the horrendous impact that the transatlantic slave business had on the African diaspora, and it requires justice,” Davis told the news outlet Politico.

The UK’s involvement in the slave trade began in 1562, and by the 1730s, the UK was the biggest slave trading nation in the world, according to the UK parliament’s website.

The website adds that British ships transported more than three million Africans, mainly to the UK’s North American and Caribbean colonies.

In June 2023, a report by consulting firm Brattle Group, titled Reparations for Transatlantic Chattel Slavery, argued that the UK owes reparations to 14 Caribbean countries. These include Antigua and Barbuda, the Bahamas, Barbados, British Virgin Islands, Cuba, Dominica, Dominican Republic, Grenada, Haiti, Jamaica, Puerto Rico, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia, and Trinidad and Tobago.

Reparations have been paid over slavery in the past – to the owners of slaves. In 1833, the British government agreed to compensation of 20 million pounds for slave owners for the “loss of their property” after passing legislation to abolish slavery in the British Empire, worth about 2 billion pounds ($2.6bn) today.

In March 2024, British institutions such as the Church of England also pledged to put together a 1-billion-pound ($1.35bn) fund to address its role in slavery.

But UK leaders have so far resisted engaging in discussions about paying reparations to the countries that received trafficked slaves, and where their descendants now live.

In October 2024, former UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s office said that the British government would not be paying for slavery and would also not apologise for it.

The British monarch has also not issued a formal apology for the crown’s role in the transatlantic slave trade.

Have other European colonial powers apologised for slavery?

So far, the Netherlands is the only European country to have apologised for its role in the transatlantic slave trade, in 2022. But the Netherlands ruled out paying reparations and instead established an approximately 200 million euros ($216m) fund to promote social initiatives in the Netherlands, the Dutch Caribbean and Suriname.

In March, even when the UN General Assembly voted to recognise the transatlantic slave trade as the “gravest crime against humanity”, many European nations, including the UK, abstained from voting in favour of the resolution.

How is the UK likely to respond to Jamaica’s latest petition?

During colonial rule, British merchants enslaved and forcibly transported 600,000 to 1 million Africans to Jamaica between the 17th century and the early 19th century.

In its current petition to the UK, the Jamaican government estimates that the country is owed about $10bn from Britain, but how the UK will respond to the petition is yet to be determined.

“We understand the Jamaican government is seeking a petition to be heard before the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council,” a Buckingham Palace spokesperson told reporters in the country in response to Jamaica’s inquiry on Monday.

Otele said she would be surprised if the new British Labour Party-led government decides to respond favourably to the requests made by the Jamaican government, but highlighted that the latest petition is nevertheless significant.

“It’s the first time the petition is being raised and its legal aspect is being debated, because so far we’ve only been talking about reparations in terms of financial compensation. Now we’re looking at the highest court of the land to legislate and have more than a conversation about the UK’s law on slavery,” she said, adding that this could also push other Commonwealth nations to raise such petitions with the UK.

“British society is ready to apologise. There have been conversations rolling about the matter. But the UK government’s stance has so far only favoured the elite, with them paying compensations to slave owners. So the British government needs to consider the matter and answer questions on its role in slavery.”

articles.title: Why the ‘Temu Range Rover’ is such a threat to Jaguar Land Rover
articles.summary: Job cuts come as JLR faces falling sales and intense Chinese competition while trying to switch to electric vehicles.
articles.body:
Jaguar Land Rover's decision to shed 4,000 jobs comes after the carmaker has travelled down a very rough road.

The company has seen sales fall in all of its major markets and has been dealing with the consequences of a devastating cyber-attack that paralysed production last year.

At the same time, it has invested billions in an effort to reinvent itself for an electric future, in which it is likely to face intense competition from aggressively expanding Chinese brands.

Executives have now decided a major overhaul is needed.

One of the main concerns for JLR is China. Not so long ago, it was seen as a land of opportunity for western carmakers, where the rapidly expanding middle classes seemed to have an inexhaustible appetite for upmarket foreign-badged vehicles.

JLR, along with other European brands such as BMW, Audi and Mercedes Benz, was all too willing to meet that demand, at a time when the European market was extremely crowded and growth hard to find.

Today, things are very different. The past decade has seen rapid growth among domestic Chinese carmakers, firmly backed by their government, which has been determined to make the country a leading player in electric vehicles.

This has created an environment of intense competition, in which local manufacturers have rapidly raised the bar in terms of technology and development speed.

That, combined with a slowdown in the Chinese economy and a reduction in sales overall, has made China a much more difficult market for European brands.

JLR's Chinese sales fell from a high water mark of 146,000 cars in 2017 to just 62,400 in the last financial year. At the same time, competition and a new luxury car tax have hit profit margins.

All of this has resulted in a sharp fall in revenues from the region. JLR is not alone in this; the Volkswagen Group, for example, has also seen its earnings in China pummelled – a major factor in its decision to axe 100,000 jobs by the end of the decade.

The state of the Chinese market has had another consequence for European carmakers, including JLR. Faced with cut-throat competition at home, Chinese firms such as BYD and Chery have been flexing their muscles abroad.

They have been rapidly gaining market share in the UK and Europe – with Chery's Jaecoo 7, nicknamed the 'Temu Range Rover' the third best-selling car in this country over the first half of the year.

Analysts say traditional brands will face an uphill struggle to compete with new rivals, who can sell cars more cheaply and develop them more quickly.

Jaguar Land Rover to cut 4,000 jobs over next two years

The true cost of cyber attacks - and the business weak spots that allow them to happen

The US is also a major market for JLR. In the year to the end of March 2025 it sold more than 120,000 cars there. The following year, that figure had fallen to just under 100,000.

Part of that could be attributed to the impact of the cyber attack, which heavily disrupted production in late 2025. It affected JLR worldwide and cost the company £1.9bn.

But sales and profits were also hit by the introduction of import tariffs by the US, and subsequent uncertainty over the levels of those tariffs. As automotive analyst Matthias Schmidt puts it, the company is "seeing a head-on hit each time a Land Rover rolls off a ship onto US soil".

JLR is now planning a partnership with Stellantis to build new Defender-badged vehicles in the US. These cars, which would be developed specifically for the US market, would not attract tariffs.

Then, there are energy costs, which affect JLR and its rivals. Carmakers and their suppliers are industrial businesses that use copious amounts of energy, and prices in the UK are among the highest in Europe.

According to Prof David Bailey of Birmingham Business School, "electricity is a fundamental input into modern industrial production".

"If producing a car in Britain is structurally more expensive because the energy required to manufacture it is substantially more expensive, Britain is effectively imposing a competitiveness tax on its own industry."

All of these challenges have come at a time when JLR has been ploughing money into the development of a new generation of electric vehicles. The first fruits of the £15bn programme were seen last week, with the official unveiling of the first electric Range Rover.

That was relatively uncontroversial – but so far the relaunch of Jaguar as an all-electric brand has been anything but. In late 2024 the company drove straight into the heart of the culture wars with a polarising advertising campaign that some saw as excessively "woke". The first actual car is due to make its public bow on 6 October – and it will be a pivotal moment for the company.

It is easy to see why JLR's chief executive PJ Balaji feels action is necessary to trim costs and make the company leaner. That is bad news for employees, with thousands of jobs to go and compulsory redundancies not being ruled out.

But the carmaker's network of suppliers are also being squeezed.

"JLR has been pushing hard for cost savings", one leading supplier told the BBC. "But those suppliers are also facing high energy costs and high employment costs…there's huge anxiety right now."

articles.title: ‘Breaks my heart’: Yemen jab shortages spark fears for millions of children
articles.summary: Some five million Yemeni children are deprived of essential routine vaccinations amid disputes.
articles.body:
Mirsal Adel, 47, had never struggled to find vaccines for his children. In his hometown of Ibb, in southwestern Yemen, public hospitals and paediatric clinics always provided them free of charge.

But when it came to vaccinating his fifth child, a four-month-old boy, securing a shot was far from straightforward.

“I visited the hospital more than once, and I was told that UNICEF, which used to provide the vaccines, stopped supplying them, with no word on when they might arrive,” said Adel.

In October 2025, the United Nations children’s agency, UNICEF, halted operations in areas controlled by the Houthis following the detention of dozens of UN staff members – including UNICEF workers – and raids on its premises . The Houthis have been fighting Yemen’s internationally recognised government for years, and have periodically cracked down on aid sector workers.

The Health Ministry in Yemen’s Houthi-held capital, Sanaa, confirmed to Al Jazeera that the final vaccine shipment it received arrived on September 4, 2025. In late July 2026, the government’s Health Ministry in Aden warned that nearly five million children in Houthi-controlled areas had been cut off from essential routine immunisations.

“Our children’s health is a red line, and we must do everything we can to get them vaccinated,” said Adel, who decided last week to travel with his son to Taiz, a government-held city some 75km (47 miles) away, where vaccines are still available.

He said the trip cost him about $100, a prohibitive expense for many families in impoverished Yemen.

“Vaccination teams used to go door-to-door to vaccinate children, but this year everything changed suddenly, and getting a reliable vaccine now costs a lot,” said Adel, who works as a treasurer at a local company. “Today, not everyone can afford the travel expenses to get their children vaccinated.”

Although he is relieved to have secured the two initial doses of polio and pneumococcal vaccinations, he is already anxious about any upcoming trips. “I hope children’s vaccines will be available locally next time so I won’t have to resort to travelling again,” he said.

The war in Yemen broke out in late 2014, when the Houthis seized much of northern and western Yemen, including Sanaa, prompting a Saudi-led coalition of Arab countries to intervene in support of the internationally recognised government in March 2015. A United Nations-brokered ceasefire in 2022 significantly reduced fighting, but tensions have escalated since July, with fighting growing fiercer in recent days.

In March this year, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs said that only 59.3 percent of Yemen’s health facilities remained fully functional, while overall complete vaccination coverage stood at 63 percent.

The figures, however, reflect the conditions before the total exhaustion of vaccine supplies in Houthi-controlled areas by July, meaning current national coverage rates are likely significantly worse.

Anees al-Asbahi, spokesperson for the Health Ministry in Sanaa, blamed UNICEF and Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, for the collapse of the vaccine supply. He said authorities had informed both agencies early on regarding the impending shortages, yet no action was taken before all nine routine childhood vaccines were entirely exhausted.

“The primary reason for the disappearance of childhood vaccines is the politicisation of humanitarian work,” he said, repeating an accusation made by the Houthis against UN agencies, particularly following last year’s decision to relocate their operations to Aden.

“Since UNICEF halted its operations in Sanaa for political reasons, they stopped supplying us with vaccines,” he added. “Furthermore, because we live under a blockade by Saudi Arabia, we cannot import them ourselves.”

When contacted by Al Jazeera, UNICEF Yemen declined to comment on the allegations, saying only that it is doing its best to help every child access vaccines. Al Jazeera also contacted Gavi for comment, but received no response.

Meanwhile, the UN continues to demand the immediate release of dozens of its personnel, alongside staff from international and local humanitarian organisations currently detained by the Houthis. The UN has also called for the return of assets seized during raids on its offices, and the lifting of operational restrictions on aid groups and their personnel.

The Health Ministry in Aden said in late July that it had sufficient vaccines for the entire country, including Houthi-controlled areas. However, it accused the Houthis of creating obstacles that prevent the receipt and transport of these supplies from government-controlled areas.

“Vaccines designated for all governorates of the Republic, including those under Houthi control, are available through health sector partners in accordance with approved international supply mechanisms,” it said. “However, the ongoing restrictions and obstacles imposed by the Houthis – which hinder their receipt, transportation and distribution according to technical standards – have prevented them from reaching the targeted children.”

Ali al-Waleedi, the deputy health minister in Aden, said the ministry had planned to carry out two polio vaccination rounds this year but accused the Houthis of not cooperating.

“The Houthis refused to accept vaccines designated for areas under their control and have shown no willingness to resolve the crisis,” al-Waleedi told Al Jazeera. “They rejected the vaccines, even though it had been agreed to allocate more than 65 percent of the total supply to areas under their control.”

Responding to the allegations regarding the rejection of shipments, al-Asbahi said there has been “no coordination” with the ministry in Aden. “We cannot accept shipments arriving by road, as they could be spoiled. UNICEF and Gavi are responsible for this, and they must uphold their responsibility to provide our children with vaccines.”

While the two health ministries present different accounts, parents such as Mohammed Abdulwahed wait for the rival authorities to reach an agreement and restore access to paediatric vaccines.

“There was a shortage of vaccines earlier this year, and we used to struggle to get them, but now we cannot find them at all in Sanaa,” said Abdulwahed. “I know some families are travelling to government-controlled areas, but that costs a lot, and I simply can’t afford it.”

Thikra, a healthcare worker who has served on door-to-door vaccination teams and currently works at a vaccination clinic in a Taiz hospital, said that dozens of children from Houthi-controlled areas were arriving at the facility each day to be vaccinated.

“It breaks my heart to see children deprived of essential vaccines while authorities in Sanaa and Aden exchange blame,” she said.

“Political issues should be kept completely separate from children’s health, and both ministries must find a solution so all children can access free vaccines,” she said, stressing that immunisation is a basic right for every child.

“I urge the international community to step in, as the next generation could suffer severe health consequences if an urgent solution is not found to restore vaccine supplies.”

articles.title: In 2019, artist Klaus Littmann filled an Austrian football stadium with 299 trees, turning it into a forest to show a future without forests
articles.summary: Rest of World News: On the pitch of Austria's Klagenfurt’s Wörthersee Stadium, where footballers would normally chase a ball beneath floodlights, 299 mature trees once st.
articles.body: On the pitch of Austria's Klagenfurt’s Wörthersee Stadium, where footballers would normally chase a ball beneath floodlights, 299 mature trees once stood in near silence. In 2019, Swiss artist and curator Klaus Littmann transformed the Austrian arena into a temporary forest, replacing the familiar spectacle of sport with a landscape of birch, oak, hornbeam, willow and other Central European trees. The trees, some reaching about 14 metres and weighing up to six tonnes, filled roughly 7,200 square metres of the stadium pitch. Visitors did not walk among them. They sat in the stands and watched the forest below as though it were the event. The installation, titled FOR FOREST – The Unending Attraction of Nature, was conceived as an unsettling question about what happens when something as ordinary as a forest becomes rare enough to require a special place to see one.A football stadium became a place to watch treesThe transformation was powerful because almost nothing about the stadium changed except what occupied the pitch. The seats remained. The grandstands remained. The architecture remained recognisably that of a football arena. What disappeared was the game. Instead, spectators looked across the field at a dense arrangement of living trees, a scene that felt simultaneously familiar and profoundly out of place. The installation was open to the public free of charge from 8 September until 27 October 2019, and visitors viewed the forest from the stands from morning until late evening. The restriction was deliberate. Littmann wanted the audience to experience the forest as something observed rather than entered. “It’s primarily about how we take things for granted,” he said. “By removing something from the familiar into a new context, you raise new questions.”The original idea was drawn almost 50 years earlierLittmann did not invent the strange image of people sitting in a stadium to watch a forest. The idea came from Austrian artist Max Peintner’s drawing The Unending Attraction of Nature, created in 1970 and 1971. Peintner’s work depicted a stadium containing trees while the outside world appeared heavily urbanised and industrialised. The people in the stands were not watching a football match but observing the remaining traces of nature below, as though a forest had become a spectacle. Littmann encountered the drawing decades later and became determined to recreate it in physical form. He eventually found the opportunity to turn Peintner’s unsettling vision into a real landscape in Klagenfurt.The forest was meant to feel real, not decorativeThere was a practical challenge behind the visual shock. Littmann wanted the stadium to contain what looked like an actual mixed woodland rather than a giant collection of ornamental plants. Swiss landscape architect Enzo Enea oversaw the selection and transplantation of mature trees, creating a composition intended to resemble a Central European forest. The species included silver birch, alder, aspen, white willow, hornbeam, field maple and oak. Because the trees were already mature, their scale changed the stadium dramatically. From the upper tiers, the pitch no longer resembled a landscaped sports ground with a few trees added to it. It looked as though a woodland had somehow taken possession of the entire playing field.The unsettling part was that nobody could enter itA conventional public forest invites people to walk beneath the canopy, touch the bark and follow paths between the trees. FOR FOREST denied that experience. Visitors remained spectators. From the stands, they could see the crowns moving in the wind and the forest changing with the season, but the pitch was not theirs to explore. The restriction reinforced Peintner’s original idea that nature might eventually be something people simply go somewhere to look at. Littmann was explicit that the project was not intended as entertainment in the ordinary sense. “It’s not about playing around in the forest,” he said. Instead, the unusual setting was meant to make people reconsider something they normally encounter without thinking about it.It was a warning about a world where forests become exhibitsThe installation’s environmental message was deliberately indirect. It did not depict dying trees, burning landscapes or a devastated ecosystem. It showed a healthy forest, but in the wrong place. That reversal was the warning. Littmann’s project description says the work sought to challenge perceptions of nature and question its future, while reminding people that nature, which is often taken for granted, might someday survive only in specially designated spaces. Austrian broadcaster ORF similarly described the project as a warning connected to climate change. The stadium was not supposed to represent an actual future location for forests. It was a visual metaphor for the possibility that intact nature could become so diminished that people would experience it as an attraction.The reaction was as much about the idea as the treesThe installation quickly became a global talking point because its image was almost impossible to forget. A football stadium is built around crowds, noise and competition, yet FOR FOREST made stillness the spectacle. Austrian public broadcaster ORF reported that around 100 journalists from around the world attended the press presentation, while the completed installation drew nearly 200,000 visitors during its two-month run. More than 8,000 people came on the final day. The project also generated controversy in Klagenfurt, including criticism over the football club having to play some matches elsewhere and questions about transporting trees from nurseries outside Austria. Those objections became part of the story because they exposed the tension between an environmental message and the practical footprint of creating a large temporary artwork.The trees themselves had a future after the stadiumThe forest was always temporary, but the trees were not intended to be disposable props. After the exhibition closed on 27 October, all 299 trees were removed from the stadium and moved to Lower Austria. Contemporary ORF reporting said they would be replanted there and form the basis of a future FOR FOREST Campus. The move also highlighted an important distinction between the artwork and the living material used to create it. The stadium forest lasted only weeks as an installation, but the trees were being treated as living organisms with a future beyond the exhibition.Nearly five decades later, Peintner’s warning had become a real placeWhat made FOR FOREST so striking was the gap between the original drawing and its eventual realisation. A disturbing image made in 1970 and 1971 had spent decades as an idea before Littmann recreated it at enormous scale in an Austrian football stadium. Peintner had imagined spectators looking at trees where a team should have been. Littmann made that scene physically possible, filling a real stadium with a forest and asking a modern audience to look at it from the stands. In a media reel for the project, Peintner described the original scene as people observing a forest instead of watching a team, with almost nothing moving except the leaves in the wind.The image ultimately worked because it did not tell visitors what a future without forests would look like. It showed them something more subtle and unsettling. A forest had survived, but had become an object of spectatorship. Nature had not vanished from the stadium. It had vanished from where people expected it to be. By placing 299 living trees on a football pitch, Littmann turned an ordinary sporting venue into a thought experiment about scarcity, memory and the value of landscapes that people often assume will always exist. For two months in 2019, one of Austria’s most recognisable public spaces became a place where the main attraction was not a match, a concert or a celebrity, but the simple presence of trees.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI:  The Election Commission on Monday announced bypolls for five Assembly constituencies and one Lok Sabha seat, with polling scheduled for Oc.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Election Commission on Monday announced bypolls for five Assembly constituencies and one Lok Sabha seat, with polling scheduled for October 6 and counting of votes on October 9.The Assembly constituencies going to polls are Nandigram and Rejinagar in West Bengal, Dharapuram and Madurantakam in Tamil Nadu, and Thattanchavady in Puducherry. The Nagaon Lok Sabha constituency in Assam will also see a bypoll.Nandigram among key contestsThe Nandigram Assembly seat was vacated by West Bengal CM and BJP leader Suvendu Adhikari, who had won the constituency in the 2026 Assembly election. He retained the Bhabanipur seat, from where he defeated Trinamool Congress chief Mamata Banerjee.The Rejinagar seat fell vacant after its MLA Humayun Kabir resigned from the constituency. In Assam, the Nagaon Lok Sabha seat was vacated after Pradyut Bordoloi resigned before the Assembly election and subsequently joined the BJP, according to reports.EVMs, VVPATs to be usedThe EC said EVMs and VVPATs will be used at all polling stations for the bypolls. It said adequate numbers of machines have been made available and necessary measures have been taken to ensure smooth conduct of polling.The ECI statement reads, "The Model Code of Conduct shall come into force with immediate effect in the district(s) in which the whole or any part of the Assembly constituency going for election is included, subject to provision of the instruction vide Commission’s letter No. dated 2nd January, 2024."Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: 3 stabbed in Brooklyn hours before West Indian American Day Parade; 1 critical
articles.summary: US News: Three men were injured in a stabbing incident in Brooklyn just hours before the West Indian American Day Parade, leaving one victim in critical condition. The incident occurred near Carroll Street and Utica Avenue, intensifying security concerns as thousands gather for the cultural celebration.
articles.body: Three men were stabbed in Brooklyn early Monday, with one left in critical condition, before the West Indian American Day Parade and J’Ouvert Festival began in Crown Heights.The attack happened around 5:48 a.m. near Carroll Street and Utica Avenue in Crown Heights, according to police reported by The New York Post.A 32-year-old man and a 23-year-old man suffered stab wounds to the neck, while a 36-year-old man was stabbed in the face.Emergency crews took all three men to Kings County Hospital. The 32-year-old remained in critical condition, while the other two victims were listed in stable condition.Police said no arrests had been made.The stabbing occurred only blocks from the J’Ouvert Festival, which was due to begin at 6 a.m. and continue until the main parade started at 11 a.m.The NYPD had already announced a major security operation for the Labor Day celebrations, with thousands of officers deployed along the parade route and in surrounding neighbourhoods from Sunday night through Monday.The main parade is scheduled to end at 5:30 pm, with the earlier finish announced after six people were shot during last year’s celebrations.“This is one of our department’s largest deployments of the year at this time,” NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch said Friday, adding that officers would be stationed throughout the parade routes and nearby areas.The West Indian American Day Parade is New York’s largest Caribbean cultural celebration. The 2026 event is the 59th annual edition and will feature J’Ouvert, masquerade bands, soca and calypso performances along Eastern Parkway under the theme “MAS.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Arizona man who got duct-taped on an American Airlines flight was VP of realty firm, company says he is no longer associated
articles.summary: US News: 67-year-old Arthur Lundeen, the man who was duct-taped to his seat on an American Airlines flight after he created a nuisance, has been fired from the.
articles.body: 67-year-old Arthur Lundeen, the man who was duct-taped to his seat on an American Airlines flight after he created a nuisance, has been fired from the real estate company where he was the VP -- after the incident. The flight from Dallas to Newark had to be diverted to Baltimore last week as Lundeen started using racial and homophobic slurs on the flight. Lundeen was arrested after the flight landed and faces state charges including second-degree assault and disorderly conduct. The FBI is also investigating the incident and could pursue federal charges, authorities said.Long Realty, a Tucson-based real-estate company, said it terminated its affiliation with Lundeen after learning about the incident. “Long Realty is aware of reports concerning criminal charges filed against a former affiliated real estate agent arising from an incident that allegedly occurred during a commercial flight," the company said in a statement. “The conduct described in the reports is wholly inconsistent with the professionalism, integrity, compassion, and respect for others that Long Realty expects from those affiliated with the company,” the statement read.Lundeen's LinkedIn profile identified him as a vice president at Long Realty in Tucson, although his profile was subsequently removed from the company's website. Long Realty said Lundeen was no longer associated with the company and was not authorised to represent it. “Long Realty promptly ended its affiliation with the individual,” the company said, adding that it had “no tolerance” for conduct that falls short of its professional standards.According to reports, Lundeen was travelling aboard American Airlines Flight 618 on Thursday night when he allegedly became increasingly belligerent toward passengers and crew.Major chaos inside flight, whoever intervened got pushed by LundeenA fellow passenger, Juan Mejia, a former law enforcement officer, told ABC News that Lundeen was sitting two rows behind him when the disturbance began. Mejia said Lundeen directed derogatory remarks and racial slurs at airline staff and other passengers and used offensive language toward women sitting nearby. The situation escalated after a flight attendant intervened. Lundeen allegedly directed a racial slur at the Black flight attendant and also made anti-gay remarks.He was also accused of physically striking his seatmate and damaging a computer during the confrontation. When another female passenger attempted to intervene, Lundeen allegedly pushed her.Several passengers eventually stepped in to restrain him.Dramatic images from inside the aircraft showed Lundeen with his hands, torso and head restrained using duct tape, while his wrists were bound with zip ties.The flight was diverted to Baltimore because of what American Airlines described as a “disruptive customer”. Law enforcement officers met the aircraft after it landed and removed the passenger before the flight continued to Newark.Maryland Transportation Police arrested Lundeen, while the FBI later confirmed that it was investigating the incident.“The FBI is currently conducting interviews to gather the facts and will consult with the US Attorney’s Office for the District of Maryland to determine if federal charges will be filed,” the agency said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1918, three Indiana brothers opened a bicycle and tire shop; 108 years later, the same family still runs it, with six employees retiring after 40+ years and tenures reaching 50 years
articles.summary: US News: An Indiana tyre and bicycle business started by three brothers in 1918 is still operating under the same family ownership 108 years later. The busines.
articles.body: An Indiana tyre and bicycle business started by three brothers in 1918 is still operating under the same family ownership 108 years later. The business has also built an unusually loyal workforce, with several employees staying for more than four decades. A report published by local news outlet The Addison Times highlights the business's long history. Along with remaining in the same family for more than a century, the firm has kept a remarkably stable workforce. Six long-serving employees have retired after more than 40 years with the company, while some workers have stayed for as long as 50 years. The business was founded during the final months of the First World War, when three local brothers opened a small shop serving motorists and cyclists across rural Indiana.Over a century of family ownershipFounded in 1918, the business first focused on repairing bicycle frames, fixing rubber inner tubes and fitting basic pneumatic tyres to early motorcars travelling on Midwestern roads. Over the decades, the shop expanded its services and adapted to major changes in the automotive and transport industries while staying connected to its original community. Ownership has been passed through several generations of the same family, preserving the founders' original approach to running the business. This continuity has been matched by a workplace culture that encourages employees to stay for many years, creating a level of job stability that is uncommon in today's retail and service industries. Data reported by The Addison Times shows how important employee loyalty has been to the company's survival. Over the years, six different workers have retired after spending more than 40 years on the payroll.Deep roots and half-century tenuresSome employees have shown an even greater level of loyalty, spending as long as 50 years with the business. These workers have seen generations of customers come and go, servicing cars and bicycles belonging to the children and grandchildren of the shop's earliest customers. Local historians and business analysts say family-owned independent shops remain important parts of rural and small-town communities in America. Major retail chains and online businesses have replaced many independent service outlets across North America over the past 50 years. However, strong customer loyalty and experienced employees have helped this Indiana business continue operating successfully. The shop's 108-year history has covered some of the biggest events and changes in American history, including the 1918 influenza pandemic, the Great Depression, the industrial effort during the Second World War and the rapid move towards digital shopping and electric transport.Maintaining community tiesAccording to The Addison Times, the shop continues to combine traditional repair skills with modern diagnostic equipment. Employees who have worked there for many years have also helped train younger mechanics, passing on practical repair skills that may not always be taught through modern corporate training programmes. Reaching 108 years of continuous operation while remaining under one family's ownership puts the Indiana business among a small group of historic American retail establishments.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1974, a California college student built a cabin using only hand tools because his father said, ‘no electricity’; 52 years later, it sits inside a $6M estate with a runway, helipad and 82-ft pool
articles.summary: US News: Kenneth Roebbelen’s luxury estate now features a 9,800-sq-ft main house, along with a 2,200-sq-ft recreation centre, an 82-ft Junior Olympic lap pool,.
articles.body: Kenneth Roebbelen’s luxury estate now features a 9,800-sq-ft main house, along with a 2,200-sq-ft recreation centre, an 82-ft Junior Olympic lap pool, a private runway, an aircraft hangar and a helipad, the Sacramento Bee reported. But half a century ago, this sprawling property in the Sacramento area looked different. It started with a small cabin, completely built using hand tools.From a hand-built cabin to an empireKenneth Roebbelen’s father, Hans Roebbelen, bought the Sacramento-area estate in the late 1960s. In 1974, Kenneth Roebbelen graduated from UC Davis; he wanted to avoid dorm living. So when he started to build a cabin, his father had one condition attached to it, which made the project part construction job and part character test.“The rule was I had to only use hand tools, no power tools, no electricity,” Roebbelen said. During weekends, he would come over to build the cabin, so he would have a place to live instead of renting an apartment after college. The 1974 cabin stands even today and is now part of the complex that grew with Roebbelen’s career, family and landholding. Kenneth Roebbelen is the former president of his family-owned Roebbelen Contracting Inc., founded by his father, Hans Roebbelen, in 1959. The family eventually owned 623 acres of land stretching to Folsom Lake. Today, the gated estate in El Dorado Hills covers 48 acres and is on the market for $6 million.What the buyer getsRoebbelen raised three children with his wife, Kimberly, in homes built gradually around that original hand-built cabin. The main residence was built between 2008 and 2010. The pool house and the pool arrived in 2024. The trick, he said, was making each era look like it belonged to the others all along. “You’re doing all this stuff in different phases of your life, and part of the goal is to make it look like it was done at one time. That it was all coordinated,” he told the outlet.This aesthetic is also deeply woven into the physical fabric. The main residence features cherrywood ceilings, Brazilian cherry floors, hydronically heated floors and carved mahogany double doors. A staircase rises more than 40 feet; carved mahogany double doors open into foyers flooded with light, and hydronically heated floors are fitted beneath it all. The primary suite has dual walk-in closets. It comes with a soaking tub, steam shower, dry sauna and private fitness area.The main entrance has wrought-iron double doors leading into an elaborate foyer with a soaring ceiling and custom stone floors. There is an art gallery that runs through the house and connects its different sections: the original cabin, older portions and the newer main house upstairs.The most striking feature is something else: mahogany wine cellar doors, intricately carved in Monterrey, Mexico, lead to a cellar that can house 2,300 bottles. A freezer salvaged from Sacramento High School’s renovation when Roebbelen was still in high school now serves as the walk-in refrigerator. It’s nearly a century old, according to him.The unique estate also has a 9,800-square-foot main residence, a 2,200-square-foot pool house anchored by an 82-foot Junior Olympic lap pool, a spring-fed fishing pond, an airstrip with a hangar, a helipad and enough amenities to rival a small resort.There is a six-car garage, storage for RVs and boats, and also a massive fertile garden built during the COVID-19 pandemic. It is nothing less than a commercial-grade greenhouse.Bronze mustangs titled ‘Spirit of Nevada’ greet visitors at the entry gate, a work by Auburn sculptor Doug Van Howd. There’s more art across the estate. For instance, a striking statue of a woman dressed in a white dress, created by Ken Shutt, overlooks the water of the expanded pond.A solar system producing 38 kilowatts, paired with ten Tesla batteries, generally offsets the property’s electricity consumption, though the pool house occasionally tips the balance. A metal roof, extensive stonework and granite hardscape speak to investment beyond the visual. The runway his father installed as an avid pilot remains; when Roebbelen ran the construction company, it let him reach Western jobs and return home the same day via pilot project managers.Beyond its size and resort-level amenities, the kind of work that’s nearly impossible to replicate at current costs, let alone afford. According to the listing agent, the $6 million asking price is a great deal. “To build this today would be $15 million. I mean, you couldn’t do it. It’s absolutely worth every nickel,” listing agent Chris Wolfe of eXp Realty told the outlet.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Thousands turn out in Serbia for funeral of  'Butcher of Bosnia' Ratko Mladić
articles.summary: Mladić was jailed for genocide during the 1990s Bosnian war and the EU warned Serbia not to glorify the convicted war criminal.
articles.body:
Thousands of people have turned out in Serbia's capital, Belgrade, to attend the funeral of the convicted war criminal Ratko Mladić.

Widely known as the Butcher of Bosnia, Mladić died at the age of 84 while serving a life sentence in the UN prison in The Hague, the Netherlands.

He was found guilty of genocide by a UN war crimes tribunal for his role in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, when around 8,000 Bosniak Muslim men and boys were killed. It was described as Europe's worst atrocity since World War Two.

A Serbian government minister had initially said that Mladić would be given a state funeral ​but those plans were changed after objections from some European leaders. On Monday, the EU denounced Mladić's "glorification".

"Ratko Mladić was a convicted war criminal who had committed war crimes, genocide, and crimes against humanity," the EU said in a statement.

"Any glorification of war criminals, genocide denial and revisionism contradict the most fundamental European values and have no place in the EU or in EU candidate countries," the statement said.

Serbia has been a candidate to join the EU since 2012, even though membership talks have recently stalled.

Ratko Mladić commanded Bosnian Serb forces in the 1990s against the Bosnian Croat and Bosniak (Bosnian Muslim) armies.

During the 1992-1995 Bosnian war, his troops committed what became known as "ethnic cleansing" in Bosnia-Herzegovina in a bid to expel the non-Serbian population by force. They besieged the capital city of Sarajevo, with the deaths of more than 10,000 people.

Mladić was arrested in 2011, 16 years after he was first indicted, and sentenced to life in prison in 2021 after a nine-year trial.

Despite his conviction for genocide, Mladić remains a national figure perceived by many Serbs as a heroic defender of the nation.

Many Serb nationalists see him as a hero and protector, particularly in the Bosnian Serb entity of Republika Srpska, where his death sparked vigils.

Several Serbian government ministers joined the crowds paying tribute outside the church where Mladić lay in state before the burial, including the Defence Minister Bratislav Gašić, and the Minister of Justice Nenad Vujić, local media reported.

The funeral service was led by the head of the Serbian Orthodox Church, Patriarch Porfirije, who said Mladić's name would remain "deeply etched in the memory and prayers of the majority of our Serbian Orthodox people, who feel and nurture a deep sense of gratitude towards him".

Early in the day, long queues formed outside the small St Luka church, as people waited to go in and pay their respects to the coffin. Many of those in the crowds were army veterans and some men were draped in flags printed with his picture on.

Crowds arrived several hours before the funeral began to light candles outside the church, accompanied by a choir on a loudspeaker in the sunshine.

Inside the church, Mladić's coffin was guarded by several men, mainly war veterans, while his wife, son, and grandchildren stood inside receiving condolences.

In a sign of the reverence held for the former general, his coffin was flown back to Serbia last week on a government plane, and was carried from the plane by six soldiers and draped in flags.

Free bus services were organised from Bosnia and most towns in Serbia for anyone who wanted to pay their respects.

On Sunday night, fans of the Serbian football club Red Star Belgrade unveiled a display of Mladic before their derby win over Partizan Belgrade.

For others, the funeral has rekindled painful memories of the war.

A woman in Sarajevo called Zdravka Gvozdjar - whose nine-year-old son was killed by Mladić-led forces during the siege of the city - told Reuters news agency it was "really horrible" that the funeral was taking place in Belgrade.

Mladić "deserved to be erased from memory for good, not to be... promoted as a hero," she said.

"He should be remembered only as a butcher."

Thousands attended the funeral because he "remains a figure of national pride and defiance," said Daniella Peled, Editor at the Institute of War and Peace Reporting NGO - who covered Mladić's war crimes trial in detail.

The war crimes tribunal "provided an incredibly detailed historical record of Mladić's crimes," she told the BBC, but the Serbian media and education system "has not reflected the true scale of his crimes or the perspectives of victims and survivors."

Pro-government Serbian media "depict him as a loyal soldier who simply carried out his duties," Peled said.

"It's extremely challenging for post-conflict societies to undertake a national reckoning or acknowledge responsibility for the crimes of the past."

articles.title: Germany’s AfD wins in key state: Is far-right on cusp of national rule?
articles.summary: The AfD, classified as ‘far-right extremist’ by Germany’s intelligence agency, is projected to come first in 2029.
articles.body:
For the first time since World War II, a far-right party is within reach of power at state level in Germany, after coming first in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday.

The Alternative for Germany (AfD) won 44 percent of the vote, stopping short of an overall majority but making clear its wide political significance.

On election night, AfD’s leader in the state called on other political groups to cooperate. “As a democrat, I will reach out to all those who wish to work with us to bring about a fundamental political turnaround,” Ulrich Siegmund said.

Yet, forming a government will prove difficult. The AfD has been classified as “far-right extremist” by the domestic intelligence agency and other political groups remain wary of striking an alliance.

The AfD has dismissed accusations of extremism and mainstream parties have been unable to halt its surge in the polls over recent months. Latest polling indicates the party, which stands for strong restrictions on immigration, restoring ties with Russia, cutting support to Ukraine and quitting the euro, is Germany’s most popular at national level.

The Saxony-Anhalt election could be a harbinger of a historic return of the far-right in the 2029 national election, when forecasts say the AfD stands a realistic chance of finishing first.

Siegmund, the charismatic 35-year-old who attracted thousands to his campaign rallies, said AfD “made history”.

“The people have made it absolutely clear that they finally want political change and, above all, they have shown that they want it with ⁠us,” he told supporters.

The AfD achieved its best-ever election result in Saxony-Anhalt with 44 percent of the vote, leaving all other parties far behind. The incumbent centre-right Christian Democrats (CDU), led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz, scored less than half of that share with 17 percent.

The AfD is projected to gain 39 of the 83 seats in the state parliament in Magdeburg, leaving it three short of the 42 needed for an absolute majority.

That means the party must find allies, but all other mainstream parties refuse to work with the far-right, a strategy of non-cooperation known as the “firewall”. The AfD has so far never participated in a governing coalition in Germany’s 16 states nor in its federal government.

While he now appears willing to strike deals with other parties to come to power, previously Siegmund signalled unwillingness to find middle ground with other political groups. Leading up to the vote, he stated that he was only interested in governing alone to bring about fundamental political change in Germany.

The election takes the AfD one step closer to advancing its agenda, while also reflecting the growing unpopularity of Germany’s ruling coalition.

In Saxony-Anhalt, the party more than doubled its vote share — from 21 percent in the last election. By contrast, the CDU’s vote halved from 37 percent to 17 percent, its worst result ever in the east-central German state.

Federal elections last year similarly resulted in a landmark performance by the AfD, which emerged as the largest opposition faction in the Bundestag, the German federal parliament in Berlin. The party came second with 21 percent of the vote, securing its highest-ever showing.

In state elections in Baden-Wurttemberg and Rhineland-Palatinate earlier this year too, the AfD more than doubled its seats — though it still finished third. In 2024, the AfD emerged victorious in the Thuringia state election and second in the Brandenburg state election — both were firsts for the party.

The AfD’s electoral gains in Saxony-Anhalt mirror growing dissatisfaction among voters — especially in the former East Germany — about the stagnant economy, high unemployment and domestic security, which the party largely pins on immigration.

Since its formation in 2013, the AfD has been embroiled in various scandals and has faced major controversies, including alleged foreign espionage links, secret deportation plans and internal nepotism.

The party went from a fringe Eurosceptic group to the country’s most powerful opposition force in little more than a decade, becoming too extreme even for the European Parliament’s far-right Identity & Democracy group. It kicked the party out in May 2024 after lead AfD candidate Maximilian Krah stated that not everyone in the SS – Adolf Hitler’s infamous Nazi paramilitary organisation – was a criminal.

Krah has also been under investigation by German prosecutors for alleged illegal payments, bribery and money laundering linked to China and Russia. The German parliament last year decided to lift the far-right legislator’s immunity to help investigators.

AfD politicians have also come under fire for employing family members, including in Saxony-Anhalt, where several parliamentarians are reported to have employed relatives.

Bundestag President, Julia Klockner, banned seven AfD employees from entering the German parliament over security concerns, after they failed internal background reliability checks due to their ties to right-wing extremist networks and past criminal convictions.

Senior AfD figures also faced a backlash for attending a secretive meeting to discuss mass deportation plans for people with a migration background.

What are the AfD’s prospects for the national election in 2029?

Pollsters are unanimous in forecasting the AfD as the largest party in Germany in the next national election in 2029, with around 28 percent of the vote.

That would mark a major transformation in the German political landscape from 2025, when the CDU and its ally the Christian Social Union together won 28.5 percent of the vote.

Yet even that outcome would not necessarily give AfD the ability to govern. If other parties maintain a “firewall” policy, that could prevent the far-right party from forming a coalition government.

Still, the Saxony-Anhalt election has been received by some politicians as a call for change. “Politics begins with considering reality,” Cem Ozdemir, head of government in the southwestern state of Baden-Wurttemberg and a member of the Green Party, wrote on X.

“That means the AfD is the election winner in Saxony-Anhalt. And that must mean for all democratic forces that nothing can remain as it is, and we must fundamentally reconsider our politics and our political style.”

articles.title: Self-described 'racist monster' Thomas Webster jailed after BBC investigation
articles.summary: A former tax worker is sentenced to two years for inciting hatred online.
articles.body:
Warning: This article contains graphic accounts of racist and violent language

A former tax worker who described himself as "the ultimate genocidal racist monster" has been jailed for inciting hatred online after he was exposed by a BBC investigation.

Thomas Webster was sacked by HMRC and investigated by police after comments he made to an undercover journalist in the BBC programme 'Unmasked: Extreme Far Right'.

Webster, 29, from Lapworth, Warwickshire, admitted 10 counts of stirring up racial hatred online , including ones calling for the killing and extinction of his racial "enemies".

Webster also admitted to stirring up religious hatred and another count of stirring up hatred on the grounds of sexual orientation. He was sentenced to two years at Warwick Crown Court.

In his online posts, Webster said he wanted Jewish and gay people to be tortured and executed.

Webster also said he wanted to kill all Muslims until they were "globally extinct."

In one instance, he said if a migrant hotel was placed on his road he would "prepare for murder and prison time, I am serious".

Webster was a member of the far right group Patriotic Alternative when BBC Wales Investigates' undercover reporter secretly recorded him at two of the group's events in 2024.

He was filmed saying that in his job at HMRC he liked to "deliberately" give non-white people "bad information which sounds interesting, like I'm deliberately trying to sabotage them."

Webster was dismissed by HMRC in February 2025, a month after the programme was broadcast.

The HMRC said it took breaches of its standards "extremely seriously" and had "robust processes" in place to investigate concerns.

"Where standards are not met, we act decisively," HMRC said in a statement.

"Following an internal disciplinary process, the individual concerned was dismissed from HMRC and ceased to be employed by the department in February 2025."

Talking to an undercover BBC reporter, Webster self-identified as a "white totalitarianist" who believed in "a world where white becomes the default human race... all other races will be extinct."

Describing himself as "a guy who seeks trouble" while on a hike with other Patriotic Alternative members, he boasted that he would have "crushed [the] skulls" of a group of non-white men if they had walked near to him.

Following the BBC programme, police opened an investigation and linked Webster to several social media accounts, mainly on X.

He was arrested for inciting racial hatred in September 2025 and police used details on his phone and computer to confirm the accounts were his. He was charged in July and pleaded guilty last month.

A number of the offending posts were still visible on X in the weeks after Webster pleaded guilty, as well as dozens of others in which he used the most extreme racist language.

In these additional posts, which did not form part of the charges, Webster praised Adolf Hitler and the Nazis and told several prominent politicians that they should be killed or subjected to sexual violence.

In one of his X posts, Webster described himself as a "genocidal racist monster."

He described his wishes for people of several races to be killed and in one post said "the next Hitler will be a man like me!"

After BBC contacted X about the posts, they were taken down - but the company did not comment further.

Days before Webster's sentencing, BBC News found another active Substack account appearing to belong to him.

The account shared posts discussing Webster's arrest, as well as intimate details of his personal life.

It also included several comments about race, including one calling for the "total genetic extinction" of people from South Asia.

One comment claimed that these posts were made in spite of bail conditions heavily limiting Webster's internet use and explicitly preventing him from communicating via social media.

After the BBC contacted Substack about the content, most of the posts were taken down, although one for which Webster was charged is still visible. The company did not respond further.

Warwick Crown Court heard Webster had been referred four times to the UK Government-led Prevent programme, a scheme aimed to stop people becoming terrorists.

The court also heard police found a crossbow in the attic of his property, which was still in its wrapping.

Jamie Scott, prosecuting, told the court that the CPS took a "proportionate approach" to charging him with 12 offences - but asked it be noted that there was "a raft" of similar material posted online by Webster.

His defence lawyer Susan Guest said Webster had a long-standing difficulty around social interaction and anxiety and said he became "more isolated" where his views were "reinforced rather than challenged" by people online.

"He almost lived in a bubble and this online community reinforced his views," Guest told the court.

"That bubble subsequently popped and he now has to take responsibility for those actions."

Sentencing Webster to two years, Judge Anthony Potter said he had been given numerous opportunities to show remorse and change his behaviour.

"Talk is very very cheap," he told Webster. "It has allowed you to escalate your offending and propagate the most harmful views.

"I cannot accept that there is a realistic prospect of rehabilitation in the community. I'd be failing in my public duty if I didn't sent you to custody."

Frank Ferguson, the Chief Crown Prosecutor for the CPS, said inciting racial hatred was a "very serious offence" which went "beyond any debate about freedom of speech."

"Expressing a wish for people to be killed… Jewish people, Muslim people, black people, south-asian people, immigrants and LGBTQ+ community as well… and encouraging other people to express similar views.

"It's not just about what he might do, it's what he might be encouraging others to do by his words," he said.

Det Ch Supt Alison Hurst, Head of Counter Terrorism Policing for the West Midlands, said Webster had been investigated previously for racially aggravated offences and thanked BBC Wales for bringing him to their attention again.

"Parts of the evidence from that documentary has been presented to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), which has led to the prosecution and sentencing," she said.

Webster was given a two-year sentence, where he'll serve half in prison and a year on licence.

If you or someone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this story, information about available help and support can be found via BBC Action Line .

articles.title: Cwmbran man 'pushed off pub stage' before death, inquest told
articles.summary: Phillip Ormerod was taken to hospital in critical condition and later died.
articles.body:
A 102-year-old man with dementia who was allegedly pushed at a Cwmbran pub died nearly two weeks later, an inquest has heard.

Philip Ormerod, from Cwmbran, Torfaen, was taken to hospital in a critical condition following an incident at the Crows Nest pub in the town on 1 August.

He is understood to have been visiting the pub for a drink when he went on to a stage in the venue to complain about the volume of the music.

A 56-year-old man from Llanelli, Carmarthenshire, was arrested on suspicion of inflicting grievous bodily harm, and remains on bail under investigation.

The senior coroner Caroline Saunders said the former design engineer "sustained a fall at the pub", adding that it happened "following an allegation that he was pushed".

The inquest heard he was taken to the Grange hospital with a fractured hip, however his condition deteriorated and he died on the 12 August.

The coroner said Ormerod's death was being investigated by police and that a forensic post mortem examination had taken place.

An inquest was opened but adjourned while a police investigation is carried out.

The coroner said that the inquest would not be resumed if there was a criminal prosecution, however should there be a need for a conclusion, it would take place on 26 May 2027.

Philip Ormerod's son Robert previously said his father was a "pub character" and that he wanted justice for him.

Following Ormerod's death, Det Ch Insp Shelley Comley, senior investigating officer for Gwent Police, said a criminal investigation is ongoing and urged people to "consider the impact that inaccurate or speculative comments" including "online commentary" could have.

The force is urging anyone who was at the pub between 22:00 and 23:00 BST on the night of the incident to contact them.

articles.title: Grindr to pay £26m to settle claims it allegedly shared users' HIV status
articles.summary: The long-running claim alleges Grindr breached UK privacy laws by sharing data with third parties.
articles.body:
Grindr has agreed to pay £26m to settle a lawsuit over allegations it shared users' personal information - including their HIV status - with third parties.

The world's largest LGBTQ+ dating app was sued in the High Court in 2024 over claims it misused people's personal information.

The class action suit was later served in the US, with the law firm leading the case saying it had signed up more than 11,000 claimants.

According to a US regulatory filing, Grindr will make two £13m payments to settle the claims. The firm said the settlement includes no admission of liability.

Grindr stressed the claims relate to "historical data practices" before 2020 when it was owned by Chinese firm Kunlun.

The filing submitted to the US Securities and Exchange Commission by Grindr said a settlement had been reached on 2 September.

"While Grindr disputes the allegations, it recognizes and acknowledges the distress and loss of trust expressed by some of its UK users regarding that pre-2020 period," the company said in its filing.

The firm has agreed to pay £13m to the counterparties by 31 December and a further £13m by 31 March 2027.

The claims brought more than two years ago by law firm Austen Hayes alleged Grindr had shared sensitive data with third parties for commercial purposes, breaching UK privacy laws.

It said this included information about the ethnicity and sexual orientation of its users.

People on Grindr have the option to share their HIV status along with when they were last tested - a move it says aims to reduce stigma, facilitate conversations and help users make informed health choices.

Chaya Hanoomanjee, the lawyer who led the claim, said in April 2024 claimants had "experienced significant distress" over their sensitive and private information being shared without their consent.

She said the company "owes it to the LGBTQ+ community it serves to compensate those whose data has been compromised".

Two data analytics services, Apptimize and Localytics, were identified as third parties with access to the sensitive data.

The claim said a potentially unlimited number of third parties used it to customise advertisements to Grindr's users.

It followed revelations in 2018 that Grindr had been sharing personal data, including the HIV status of its users, with the two data analytics providers.

Grindr defended the practice at the time as in line with industry standards – but it said it then stopped sharing HIV data with those companies.

It was fined £5.5m by Norway's data protection watchdog and, later in 2022, reprimanded by the UK Information Commissioner's Office for its data practices.

The company said in its filing on Friday that since 2020, it had "overhauled" its privacy practices to help meet the "unique needs of its community".

"Grindr is and remains a safe space for users, committed to transparency, user control, and responsible data practices," it said.

articles.title: Meet Mehmet Tascioglu, who started tutoring 15 students during COVID; 5 years later his nonprofit has delivered 60,000 free tutoring sessions
articles.summary: US News: When the COVID-19 pandemic forced schools to close, high school student Mehmet Tascioglu decided to act about the disruption students were facing. On .
articles.body: When the COVID-19 pandemic forced schools to close, high school student Mehmet Tascioglu decided to act about the disruption students were facing. On October 19, 2020, he helped start Connect Me with a small group of volunteers, offering free tutoring to just 15 students in the Metro-Detroit area. The idea was simple: give students access to reliable academic support at a time when normal classroom learning had been thrown into uncertainty. What began as a small local effort quickly grew far beyond southeast Michigan. After gaining attention from local media, Connect Me expanded its volunteer network, developed training and leadership programmes and began reaching students across the US and other countries. Five years later, the student-run nonprofit says it has delivered more than 60,000 free tutoring sessions, involving more than 600 volunteers and reaching 43 states and 12 countries.Student-run nonprofit earns NBC awardThe organisation's growth has also brought national recognition, including NBC's "Making a Difference" Award in 2021 and a "Be More" Grant from the National Society of High School Scholars in 2024. Connect Me describes itself as the largest student-run tutoring nonprofit organisation in the United States, while its mission remains rooted in the same principle that inspired its creation: helping students access education without the cost of traditional tutoring.The organisation's growth accelerated during its first two years. According to Connect Me, it developed leadership teams and tutor training programmes while expanding beyond southeast Michigan to connect students and volunteers across the United States and internationally. Its first major public exposure came in January 2021, when the organisation's story was covered by Hometown Life and FOX 2 Detroit. Later that year, Connect Me received NBC's "Making a Difference" Award, recognising the work of its young volunteers during a particularly difficult period for students.Connect Me strengthens free tutoring network in 2023As Connect Me expanded, the organisation moved beyond its original pandemic response and began developing a broader structure around free tutoring. In 2023, it says it launched new initiatives, expanded its Executive Team and strengthened partnerships with schools and youth organisations.Connect Me also received the "Be More" Grant from the National Society of High School Scholars in November 2024. The organisation says the grant recognised its innovation, leadership and commitment to educational equity and excellence.Connect Me delivers $5.7 million worth of free tutoringFive years after its founding, the small tutoring initiative had become the largest student-run tutoring nonprofit organisation in the United States. The website has helped more than 600 volunteers deliver over 60,000 free tutoring sessions, reaching students in 43 states and 12 countries.The organisation estimates the value of the free tutoring it has provided at more than $5.7 million. Connect Me's work is driven by volunteers with a passion for tutoring and a desire to give back to their communities, rather than by a traditional commercial tutoring model.Small high-school tutoring effort becomes an international nonprofit organisationThe scale of Connect Me's growth is striking because of how modest its beginnings were. The organisation started with a small group of high-school students trying to help 15 learners in their local community during an unprecedented disruption to education. Five years later, the same student-led model had developed into an international volunteer network. Connect Me's mission remains centred on making tutoring accessible while continuing to expand its services. articles.title: Witness says seeing Amazon plane crash at MIA was "something from a movie"
articles.summary: Five people were killed and five others were injured when a plane overshot a runway at Miami International Airport and crashed.
articles.body:
Federal investigators have descended upon South Florida to try and determine what led to a deadly incident at Miami International Airport involving an Amazon cargo plane on Sunday afternoon .

Witnesses are now starting to share their experience of what they saw and heard when the plane overshot the runway, crashed and burst into flames.

Grace Mercado said she was in a vehicle being driven by her partner when he made a chilling statement.

"We hear a noise," she said. "And he goes, 'Oh my goodness. Is that a plane crash?'"

Mercado said she looked up from her cell phone to see what he was talking about, and that's when she saw the Amazon cargo plane had overshot the runway, plowed across the Miami-Dade street and came to a stop.

"It was extremely loud," she said. "It wasn't anything that I've ever heard before. It was like a shake. Honestly, I can't compare it to anything else."

Mercado said she was disoriented trying to make sense of what she had just seen.

"The plane was up in smoke," she said. "It was just, it was like something from a movie. It was crazy."

And while first responders were nowhere to be seen at first, that changed quickly.

"There weren't any ambulances or anything," she said. "But they ended up there in under a minute. It was absolutely insane."

Dozens of units, hundreds of personnel respond to crash at MIA

According to Miami-Dade Fire Rescue , more than 60 MDFR units and about 200 personnel responded to the scene of the crash, with the first units arriving within seconds.

In total, five people were killed and five others were injured.

"Our hearts are with the victims and their families following (Sunday's) tragic cargo plane crash," Miami-Dade Fire Rescue said in a statement . "We are deeply saddened by the loss of life and are keeping everyone who was injured in our thoughts and prayers."

Mercado said that after the crash, she didn't see any movement in or near the crashed airplane, but instead just saw a lot of smoke.

"It's something you don't see in real life," she said. "So, it's surreal."

Investigators with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) will work to try and figure out why the aircraft left the runway and crashed.

The identities of the victims have not yet been released.
